https://telex.hu/english/2026/08/10/we-c.text: Menü Kereső We asked Szijjártó’s press secretary whether ministry staffers really used to be sent to his press conferences English Aradi Hanga Zsófia Andrea Horváth Kávai (translation) Állítsd be a Telexet megbízható forrásnak! Beállítom During Péter Szijjártó’s tenure as Hungarian minister of foreign affairs, staff members at the ministry were regularly sent to attend his press conferences—this is what several former and current employees of the foreign ministry told 444. After the article was published, we contacted Péter Szijjártó’s press secretary, Máté Paczolay to request a response to the publication’s claims. In response to our question, Paczolay explained in detail how they organized the briefings to ensure that all seats in the room were filled. According to 444, the minister’s office would routinely notify the heads of various departments in advance about how many staff members were expected to attend each of Szijjártó’s bilateral press briefings, and prior to the events, the department heads were required to send a list with the names of those would be in attendance. According to the publication, all of this was necessary because the invited press and the delegations accompanying foreign guests would not have filled the room on their own. Paczolay wrote that “the 444 article contains both truth and misinformation” and added that in order to get the full picture, it is important to note that Péter Szijjártó was the most active government official in terms of communication. “On a less busy day, there were one or two press events at the ministry of foreign affairs; on an average day, three or four; and on a busier day, five or six.” According to the former minister’s press secretary, it is natural that when three press events were held in a single day, “the interest of the media would wane” by the third one, but they made every effort to ensure that none of the guests of the MFA were offended by having to “deliver a speech representing their country to an even mildly empty room.” Therefore, “in such cases, they would invite staff members from the relevant specialized departments. Some took advantage of the opportunity, some did not; some came gladly, while others-apparently found it an added burden.” Paczolay emphasized that participation was not mandatory. “I don’t have the exact information on this, but I’m certain that the ministerial protocol office kept making phone calls until every last seat was filled, since that was their job,” he wrote to Telex. According to the press secretary, “the heads of the various departments also found it beneficial for a staff member responsible for a given region to hear the foreign minister of that country—for which they were, in effect, responsible within the ministry—speak in person, as well as to have the opportunity to meet with members of the delegation accompanying the foreign minister.” “So yes, the seats were always filled. Sometimes there were twenty journalists and thirty invited guests in a fifty-seat room, while at other times there were three journalists and forty-seven guests.” In its article, 444 also reported that most of the press was excluded from the briefings to begin with, and a foreign affairs staffer told the paper that they once witnessed a colleague from the press department of the ministry dictating to the reporter of the state news agency (MTI) the exact questions they should ask. We asked Paczolay whether they usually coordinated questions with the correspondents of MTI, to which he replied, “No.” “We issued press releases about each event involving Péter Szijjártó, and we streamed the entire press conference live on various online platforms, so it was very rare that MTI sent a reporter in person to the Ministry of Foreign Affairs,” he wrote. He acknowledged that they coordinated with the journalists attending the press conferences: “We always asked them whether they were going to have any questions, or whether they would address issues unrelated to the topic of the visit—usually matters of domestic politics.” He wrote that the reasons for this were practical: on the one hand, this allowed them to structure the moderation and adjust the planned duration of the press conference accordingly; on the other hand, they would inform Szijjártó in advance to expect that domestic politics would be brought up alongside bilateral issues. “This was the basic approach in our day-to-day work, but over the course of 12 years, there were countless unique situations requiring unique solutions, as we hosted guests from every corner of the world, each with different cultural customs and needs,” he wrote. 444 also reported that Gyula Budai, the ministerial commissioner responsible for measures to protect the economy, was present at every press conference, regardless of the subject. We also inquired about the reasons for this, and Paczolay wrote that since Budai was “essentially present at all of the foreign minister’s negotiations, he was a member of the delegation, and protocol dictates that members of the delegation need to attend press conferences because these are also part of the official program.” For more quick, accurate and impartial news from and about Hungary, subscribe to the Telex English newsletter! https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text: CIA director George Tenet with senior Bush administration staff at the presidential emergency operations center after the attacks of 9/11. Photograph: David Bohrer/US National Archives via Getty Images View image in fullscreen CIA director George Tenet with senior Bush administration staff at the presidential emergency operations center after the attacks of 9/11. Photograph: David Bohrer/US National Archives via Getty Images September 11 2001 ‘It was all hands on deck’: how the CIA responded to 9/11 Veterans recall chaos and confusion as the attacks unfolded – followed by a ‘war on terror’ that left agency with a tarnished reputation Robert Tait in Washington Thu 10 Sep 2026 14.11 EDT Last modified on Thu 10 Sep 2026 14.13 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google A generation of spies had lost an enemy but not yet found a role. Then came 9/11. A decade after the dissolution of the Soviet Union, al-Qaida’s devastating attacks on New York and Washington on 11 September 2001 announced to the Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) that the long era of battling communism, for which it had been founded, was officially at an end. It was to be replaced by a no-holds-barred “war on terror” that would leave the CIA with a soiled reputation over falsified intelligence that led to the invasion and occupation of Iraq, and an extraordinary rendition program in which suspects were subjected to “enhanced interrogations” at secret sites that official US inquiries subsequently defined as torture. The US intelligence community was dramatically transformed after two planes flew into the World Trade Center, a third smashed into the Pentagon, and a fourth crashed in the Pennsylvania countryside after passengers overcame the hijackers. Accounts of what unfolded inside the CIA’s headquarters in Langley, Virginia, suggests an organization unprepared for the drastically changed world the attacks ushered in, despite an awareness among some in the intelligence community that al-Qaida and its leader, Osama bin Laden , represented a clear and present danger. Margaret Henoch, then a counter-intelligence officer with little knowledge of terrorism, recalls confusion, chaos and an initial lack of direction from senior leadership as staff struggled to process what seemed like a bolt from a clear blue sky on that balmy late summer day. “One of my officers came in and said to me: ‘A plane just ran into the World Trade Center,’” she said. To this day, Henoch – who had previously been stationed in Vienna, where she focused on the International Atomic Energy Agency and nuclear threats – is haunted by the apparent vacuum that followed. View image in fullscreen Smoke pours over the lower Manhattan skyline on 9/11. Photograph: Brad Rickerby/Reuters About 40 minutes after the first attack, with no clear direction from the top of CIA, she decided to go up to the seventh floor, which accommodated the agency’s senior figures, including its then director, George Tenet . To her surprise, the area was deserted, apart from three assistants. “It was reasonable that they would have moved those guys someplace else,” said Henoch. “What was unreasonable, in my humble opinion, was that no one thought about all those people sitting in that building. Because if the Pentagon was hit, there was a chance that we, too, were a target – and it would be nice to believe that the people who left the building rapidly had a thought for all those who worked for them. “It was not clear that they did.” The Guardian contacted Tenet, now working in the private sector, for comment. In an emailed response, Bill Harlow, the CIA’s public affairs director at the time of the attacks, cited details in the 2007 memoir, At The Center Of the Storm, which he co-wrote with Tenet, and said orders were issued for the majority of the staff to leave the building at “about 10am” – nearly an hour after the second plane struck at 9.03am. Harlow added: “We were aware at the time of intelligence gathered around 1995-96 of terrorist desires to attack CIA HQ with an airplane. “Director Tenet and the senior leadership moved to another building on the compound that presented a lower profile and would have a greater chance of survival if we were hit by a plane. Notably, a decision was made that the personnel of the counter-terrorism center remained in the original headquarters building throughout that day … accepting the risk. The senior leadership team returned to the headquarters in the middle of the afternoon on 9/11.” ‘I had a briefing on who the hell al-Qaida was’ Some time afterwards, an order was given for the thousands of personnel in the building to evacuate. Some, including Henoch, were told to relocate to alternative sites to address the emergency. But by the time of that instruction, nearby roads were choked with traffic as commuters returned home from Washington DC after being released from work early. That prevented agency staff from departing, and triggered fears that they could be sitting ducks for the doomed fourth plane, which was already known to be in the air. “Large segments of the CIA operating staff were trapped,” Henoch said. “One guy, who was senior to me, was standing next to me in the car park and he said, ‘I have served in multiple war zones. I was a combat soldier in Vietnam and I’m going to die in the parking lot of the CIA.’” The dysfunctional scene was soon replaced by one of much greater conviction – leading to permanent changes in US intelligence. “I just remember loads of cable traffic coming in that said: it’s got to be al-Qaida,” said Henoch. “It wasn’t my world, so I had to have a quick briefing on who the hell al-Qaida was, because I just didn’t know anything about it. “The change was immediate. The next morning, everybody at the Central Intelligence Agency had to know who they were, and how it intersected with everything you were doing.” Steven Cash, a former CIA counter-terrorism officer who had left the agency to join the staff of the US Senate intelligence committee six months beforehand, faults the CIA’s pre-9/11 terrorism strategy as being too narrowly focused “looking to find bad guys” while neglecting the “political dimension”. View image in fullscreen Osama bin Laden in Afghanistan in April 1998. Photograph: AP “There was an emphasis on looking a terrorists as if they were a motorcycle gang,” said Cash, who had specialized on the Lebanese Shia group, Hezbollah, a close ally of Iran. “A decision was made in the first [George HW] Bush administration to take terrorism away from the people who looked at geographic areas and separate it out. [It was] illustrative of a mistaken way of looking at the world, because terrorists don’t exist in a vacuum.” Cash moved on to focus on the Balkans before leaving the agency, but still harboured guilt after the attacks. “Was this our fault? Did we fail? That kind of guilt felt, at least for me, really personal.” Cash had been on Capitol Hill, attending a committee meeting, when news of the attacks filtered through. “Somebody said, put on the TV and we saw the second plane hit,” he said. “And then they started evacuating the building. “It was a mess. People were in the hall screaming, running around. The third plane had hit the Pentagon by that point, because we could see smoke across the National Mall.” The following day, Cash and his then boss, the late Democratic senator Dianne Feinstein, visited CIA headquarters and found a mood of determined resolve. “It was all hands on deck. The people I knew were getting deployed very quickly to Afghanistan,” he recalled. “These people are pros. They didn’t care whether they were blamed or not. They wanted to do something. “I have a little bit of survivor guilt here. Maybe I should have been shipped out to Afghanistan.” Political pressure On their visit to CIA headquarters on 12 September, senators asked agency operatives what legislation and resources they would need to respond to the attacks of the previous day, according to Cash. Two early – and controversial – results were the USA Patriot Act of 2001, which expanded law enforcement and surveillance powers, and the Homeland Security Act of the following year, creating the US Department of Homeland Security, which houses agencies including Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE). Later changes established the Office of the Director of National Intelligence , with the goal of coordinating 18 different intelligence bodies and eliminating the lack of coordination widely held to blame for warning signs of the 9/11 plot going unheeded. “DNI was formed to make sure that we actually share everything with everybody. We don’t just keep it inside CIA,” said Susan Miller, a retired CIA counter-intelligence officer. View image in fullscreen George Bush with CIA director George Tenet, speaker of the House Dennis Hastert, defense secretary Donald Rumsfeld and Senate majority leader Tom Daschle on 12 September 2001. Photograph: Mark Wilson/Getty Images “What’s really cool is we’ve changed how we do things across the board, not just for terrorism. It’s really improved things. There was no coordination before.” Yet the reaction to the attacks changed intelligence in another way – by making it more susceptible to political pressure, as President George W Bush’s administration searched for information that could be used to justify an invasion of Iraq to topple Saddam Hussein. In September 2002, Henoch – who had previously studied Russian weapons capabilities working at the Stanford Research Institute – was asked to assess intelligence provided by an Iraqi defector codenamed Curveball, who had sought asylum in Germany, and provided its intelligence agency with what he said was proof of Saddam’s biological weapons program. She quickly concluded the claims were fabricated, and passed her conclusions up the chain of command. They were not well received. When Colin Powell, the then US secretary of state, visited the CIA months later to review the agency’s intelligence on Iraq, Henoch and her fellow doubters were not informed. Powell’s subsequent speech to the United Nations security council in February 2003, in which he made the case for war, relied heavily on Curveball’s testimony – despite Henoch’s insistence when the address was checked with her and other officers beforehand that his assertions were not credible. “We took a look at the Powell speech and I said: ‘You can’t use this. We think this is garbage,” she said. “I did write somewhere – I can’t remember on what page – ‘How can you send someone to die for something like this? No one ever answered that for me. “The next thing I heard was, ‘Well, when we get in there, we’ll find something.’” View image in fullscreen Tariq Aziz, Izzat Ibrahim and Taha Yassin Ramadan with Saddam Hussein, far right, in Baghdad in July 2002. Photograph: INA/Getty Images After the invasion, inspectors found no evidence of biological weapons . Curveball was later debunked as a fraud. Miller, too, encountered the administration’s zeal for intelligence that could justify invading Iraq when she was posted to Prague as CIA station chief in 2002. Czech intelligence had investigated – and, initially, tentatively confirmed – a claim that one of the 9/11 ringleaders, Mohammed Atta, had travelled to Prague the previous year and met an Iraqi embassy official, Ahmad Samir al-Ani, months before the attacks. The report was seized on by the hawkish US vice-president, Dick Cheney, as evidence of Saddam’s possible links to the attacks, thus providing another justification for war. But Czech intelligence officials retreated from their earlier stance, and the CIA concluded there was no evidence that the meeting happened. Nevertheless, Donald Rumsfeld, then the US defense secretary, brazenly tried to revive it when Miller briefed him – along with George W Bush and Condoleezza Rice, the national security adviser – when they visited the Czech capital for a Nato summit in 2002. View image in fullscreen Colin Powell, Condoleezza Rice and Donald Rumsfeld with President Bush at the Prague Nato summit. Photograph: Brooks Kraft/Corbis/Getty Images “‘Young lady, you forgot about this other thing’,” Rumsfeld told Miller, she said. “I played dumb and said: ‘What other thing?’ He replied: ‘Mohammed Atta was here in Prague meeting the Iraqi consul.’ “Bush was looking really uncomfortable and Condi was looking straight ahead. I simply said, ‘Mr President, Madam Secretary, and Mr Rumsfeld, the CIA, the Czech service and I don’t make things up. We give you the facts, and the fact is that he was not here.’ “Bush and Rice nodded in acceptance and the ambassador supported me. But Rumsfeld threw his pen down in disgust.” The invasion the neocons craved Whether the supposed meeting happened or not, Rumsfeld and his neoconservative allies got the invasion they craved – leading to a protracted conflict that tarnished the CIA’s reputation and whose length, along with the coinciding US-led military campaign in Afghanistan, spurred popular opposition to “forever wars”. Despite the blow to the agency’s standing, Cash insisted that its intelligence-gathering and functioning radically improved, thanks to the changes instituted after the attacks. “We have improved our intelligence capabilities significantly from what they were before 9/11,” he said, citing the success in preventing repeat attacks on US soil. View image in fullscreen The CIA seal at headquarters in Langley. Photograph: Dennis Brack/Bloomberg via Getty Images But with the Trump administration now engaged in a war with Iran, roiling the Middle East, such security could no longer be guaranteed, he believes. “I’m not saying it was a great time,” Cash said, of the CIA’s record in the months and years after September 2001. “But the sense of purpose of being at a place in history where we – as a group, as a society – can do something, was pretty intoxicating. “I was very proud to have been part of it. It sucked – but proud to have been part of it. And I think everything we’re seeing now is the antithesis of that.” Explore more on these topics September 11 2001 news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed US news US politics Midterms 2026 World Climate crisis Middle East Ukraine US immigration Soccer Business Environment Tech Science Newsletters The Filter Wellness

(Image credit: Getty Images/Universal History Archive / Contributor) Copy link Facebook X Whatsapp Reddit Pinterest Flipboard Threads Email Share this article 0 Join the conversation Follow us Add us as a preferred source on Google Newsletter Subscribe to our newsletter Dennis Gabor was a Hungarian-British physicist who's widely credited with inventing holography, a photographic technique that can record and reconstruct three-dimensional images. This is an invention for which he received the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1971. But his legacy extends to his philosophy on the nature of innovation "Technological and social inventions are broadening this probability space all the time; it is now incomparably larger than it was before the industrial revolution—for good or for evil. The future cannot be predicted, but futures can be invented. It was man’s ability to invent which has made human society what it is. The mental processes of inventions are still mysterious. They are rational but not logical, that is to say, not deductive." — Dennis Gabor, March 1963 Go your own way Gabor wrote this iconic passage in his now-extremely rare book 'Inventing the Future', in which he sketched out an optimistic vision for the future. Quote of the day This article is part of TechRadar Pro's QOTD project to provide an insight into the minds of the brightest and most recognized figures in the technology industry today and in years gone by. Read the full series here . At the core of his belief was that there was no need to any longer passively predict what may come to pass in the years ahead. Instead, the influence and strength of science and industry was such that mankind could forge its own future. Latest Videos From TechRadar Watch full video here: The comments also focused on that pivot point of the industrial revolution, before which the possibilities of the future were fairly limited, in his view. As each wave of innovation comes to pass, the possibilities continue to expand. Charting a path There's no understating the influence that Gabor had in modern science and industry. His comments were routinely quoted, and even adopted, by others. Chief among the figures that took this philosophy to heart was Alan Kay , described as one of the true luminaries of personal computing. You may like Quote of the day by Microsoft co-founder and ex-CEO Bill Gates: 'We always overestimate the change that will occur in the next two years and underestimate the change that will occur in the ten' — insights on the nature of progress Quote of the day by Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella: "Our industry does not respect tradition – it only respects innovation" Quote of the day by Alan Turing: 'We can only see a short distance ahead, but we can see plenty there that needs to be done' Kay, whose career spanned stints at Apple and HP among other industry titans, used this idea of inventing, not predicting, the future as a core maxim from 1971. He used the phrase to inspire his work in pioneering elements like the graphical user interface and laptops many years before they were realized. Although Gabor was a very influential figure in the technology world, his predictions weren't always on the mark . In 1962, for instance, he said sending documents via telephone wires was possible, but only in principle. That's because the equipment required was so expensive that he didn't see a world in which they'd be cheap enough for the technology to become practical. Are you a pro? https://www.wsws.org/en/articles/2026/09.text: Menu Search Latest Profile English Contact | About | International Committee of the Fourth International ( ICFI ) Menu Search International Committee of the Fourth International ( ICFI ) Latest Profile Fourth International Socialist Equality Party IYSSE About the WSWS Contact Donate European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen used her annual State of the (European) Union address to the European Parliament in Strasbourg Wednesday to unveil plans for a European security bloc operating independently of NATO. It was a declaration that the European bourgeoisie must act independently of the Trump administration to assert its predatory interests on a world scale, above all by waging war against Russia in Ukraine and a trade war against China. In a direct challenge to the US, this plan includes forming an economic and military alliance with Canadian imperialism. European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen used her annual State of the Union address to the European Parliament in Strasbourg, September 16, 2026 [Photo: © European Union 2026 - Source: EP] Quoting Charles Dickens’ description of Europe during the French Revolution, “It was the best of times, it was the worst of times,” von der Leyen declared, “The state of our Union is the strongest it has ever been” but also “as precarious as it has ever been.” Addressing Russia first, she declared that Europe faces “an openly hostile world,” in which “a territorial war of aggression is raging on our continent” and “a fight for industrial capacities is shaping global competition.” This meant alliances the EU chose were now in response “to the fracture in the international rules-based system.” In a speech never mentioning the United States, everyone knew whom she meant when hailing a Europe that “stood up for Greenland when threatened”. “In the cold fragility of today’s world,” she insisted, “only Europe can provide true sovereignty to Europeans.” That “rules-based system”—which the WSWS has analysed as “a euphemism for the right of the imperialist powers to make war on whomever they choose” —was the post-war order established under American hegemony. Washington is now tearing that order apart. Only the day before von der Leyen’s address, Washington sent EU legislators a paper threatening to revoke “Buy American” waivers for 19 member states unless “European preference” rules favouring European arms makers are scrapped from a proposed €402 billion competitiveness fund. At issue is which ruling class will pocket the profits from Europe’s rearmament—a central plank of von der Leyen’s call, with the expansion of the war against Russia pivotal to her speech. She described the discovery of a drone at Leipzig Airport, with no proof offered, as “an attack using military-grade material, carried out by Russian operatives on European soil.” Pointing to incursions on “our soil” in Denmark, Lithuania and Poland, she declared, “We should be under no illusions about what is happening here: hybrid threats facing Europe are less and less hybrid and less and less threats.” In response “Europe will defend each and every single square metre of its territory,” von der Leyen vowed. She then proposed a European Security Council, a leaders’ format “with partners like Canada, Norway, Ukraine, the United Kingdom and others involved.” It would be accompanied by an “Emergency Security Protocol” modelled on NATO’s Article 4—which allows allies to demand consultations when their security is threatened. “We are strengthening our work with NATO,” she said. “But our doctrine, our institutions and our decision-making have not kept pace with the new reality.” The EU now required “a consensus on how to respond to certain incidents. Those which fall below armed aggression but clearly threaten our national security. In other words, a mechanism to flank NATO’s Article 4.” The Euractiv website described the proposal as “a radical change to Europe’s security architecture.” The council “would emerge as a potential rival to NATO, and it’s unclear whether [NATO chief] Mark Rutte, the NATO secretary-general, or Donald Trump, the US president, would welcome such a format.” In February, von der Leyen publicly rebuked Rutte for insisting Europe could not defend itself without Washington. The European powers are hellbent on escalating the conflict with Russia. Von der Leyen delivered the Ukraine war section of her speech in German. She pledged the “strongest-ever support to Ukraine over the toughest winter of the war.” She noted that for the first time, last week, “we approved the purchase of American Patriot air defence missiles”, declaring that “these must now be delivered urgently.” However, this again exposed Europe’s continued military dependence on the US. In response von der Leyen insisted that “we must also jointly reduce our dependence on a single supplier.” Firstly, there would be the rapid development of “an affordable, modular missile-defence system with Ukraine.” Known as Freyja, this would “bring together the combat experience and innovation capacity of the Ukrainians with Europe’s technological leadership. And, of course, our substantial production capacity.” Referring to European arms spending increasing by 80 percent in five years, she boasted, “The surge in defence spending has led to record levels of investment in our capabilities and forces.” This meant “We are spending more European than ever before. Bigger orders for our industry, more interoperability and more economies of scale. Now we need to take that approach to the next level.” Von der Leyen announced “a new European Instrument for Strategic Enablers—fully aligned with NATO,” for air-to-air refuelling, strategic transport, air and missile defence, space and cyber in order to lessen reliance on US technology. Ask more questions at SocialismAI.com Trade war would accompany military readiness, with von der Leyen targeting China, who she declared was responsible for “deindustrialisation in the industrial heartlands of Europe”. A €1 billion-a-day trade deficit with Beijing had reached a “tipping point” and was “unsustainable”. With “dialogue with China to rebalance our trade” at an end, it was time for “results”. A new European Corporation on Critical Raw Materials would procure and stockpile rare earths—a trade war measure against Beijing’s dominance of supply. “Let me be clear: we will use all tools at our disposal to rebalance our relationship. Words are good. But deeds are better,” she threatened. The most naked expression of the rift with Washington was the presence in the chamber of Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney, who received a standing ovation. Carney has called for a “unique alliance” with the EU, a move critical in reducing its heavy dependence on US trade. Last month, after trade talks collapsed and Trump imposed new 50 percent tariffs, while continuing to call Canada the 51st state, Carney declared, “ You’re at war when you’re attacked, and we got attacked .” Von der Leyen directly addressed Carney saying, “Dear Mark, I said we must urgently reimagine our partnerships… so I would like to work with you on opening the door for Canada to being the first associate member of the European Union.” She continued, “We share one ocean, one set of values, one way of seeing the world. And we will now build our shared future as well”, bringing “the relationship with Canada to the highest level possible”. Underscoring the breakdown in the post-war order regulating global trade, no such associate status exists within EU treaties. Von der Leyen made the fight against Russia and trade supremacy over China central to her call for closes ties to Ottawa: “We see the world with the same eyes: from AI to climate change, from the Arctic to geopolitics. And we have stood together: on Ukraine, on defence, on raw materials and on supply chains.” Therefore, “We will move from CETA [existing Canada/EU trade deal] to an Alliance for the Future… We will integrate defence industrial bases. We will work on energy, critical minerals and batteries.” Von der Leyen’s speech was echoed by German Social Democrat MEP Bernd Lange, chair of the European Parliament’s Committee on International Trade, who said, “It is totally unpredictable what the United States are doing.” Europe must build a bloc, he stated, otherwise, in a reference to Carney’s statement at Davos earlier this year as Trump stepped up trade war measures, “you will be part of the menu.” The leader of the right-wing European People’s Party bloc Manfred Weber stated that “Putin won’t stop,” which required the creation of “joint command structures, European drones, European satellites, so closely connected that no one can ever undo this cooperation”. This was necessary so that Europe does not continue to field “27 bonsai armies.” The World Socialist Web Site is the voice of the working class and the leadership of the international socialist movement.
